entries.title: ICE to Launch Another 5,000-Person Recruitment Surge This Year
entries.summary: The expansion would boost ICE’s workforce by about 17%.
entries.content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to hire 5,000 employees before year’s end to bolster President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign, even as thousands of earlier recruits await background checks.

The expansion, according to The New York Times, would boost ICE’s manpower by about 17%, with most recruits expected to become deportation officers tasked with field arrests, detentions and managing deportation cases.

During Trump's second term, the agency has already grown by about 8,000 employees to reach a total of 29,000 people, according to federal data published in July. The latest recruitment drive comes as ICE arrests hit record highs last month.

Republicans in Congress have infused the agency with more than $100 billion via a pair of multi-year budget reconciliation packages. Between those funding spikes and intense political pressure from the Trump administration to meet strict arrest quotas, ICE’s rushed hiring efforts have already drawn criticism.

Earlier this year, new personnel were approved for work with little to no vetting, according to reports, and hundreds were subsequently fired or quit. In one case, an investigative journalist said she was able to secure a job offer from ICE after a six-minute interview and a passing drug test.

This time, Homeland Security said it will vet candidates more thoroughly, the Times reported, but it's unclear how the agency can fulfill its massive hiring goal in just three months without running into similar problems.

“Adequately vetting people takes time,” Deborah Fleischaker, a former ICE chief of staff under the Biden administration, told the Times. “It’s more important to get it right than do it fast.”

DHS officials said the hiring growth is the result of new funding and is “unrelated to attrition from the previous surge in hires,” according to the article.

entries.title: How Hakeem Jeffries Is Courting the Left
entries.summary: House Democratic leaders are trying to connect with a group of progressive candidates who have refused to support Hakeem Jeffries’ speaker bid, sources told The Washington Sun.
entries.content:
Democrats appear closer than ever to winning the House majority, and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ is already working to corral — and connect with — a growing chorus of progressive dissenters, The Washington Sun has learned.

At least six progressives who won their House primaries and will likely get elected in November have not committed to supporting Jeffries for speaker should Democrats win a majority. Even just a handful of holdouts could be enough to stand in between Jeffries and the gavel, or, as quite a few Republican speakers have learned, make life as the chamber’s leader very difficult.

Colorado’s Melat Kiros, New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy, Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb and Michigan’s Donavan McKinney have all declined to back Jeffries ahead of the November election. Jeffries and members of his leadership team have been conducting public and private outreach to the incoming cohort of progressives, according to multiple sources familiar with the conversations.

Jeffries has now spoken with all the progressives who won their primaries, and has met with or plans to meet with them all in person, one of the sources said.

Reps. Joe Neguse of Colorado and Lauren Underwood of Illinois, two members of Jeffries’ leadership team, have also conducted their own outreach to the lefty insurgents, multiple sources said. Neguse and Underwood are both angling to move up the leadership ladder in the next Congress. The calls were described as friendly and welcoming by the sources, with the congressional Democrats offering advice and support to potential new members.

Jeffries, Neguse and Underwood declined to comment on the story.

Jeffries has also signaled some movement on major issues that divide progressives from the establishment. The longtime pro-Israel Democrat said that U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East “must change” after a divisive vote over aid to Israel fractured his caucus this summer. In a letter to colleagues, Jeffries argued that Israel “is capable of paying for its own sophisticated weapons” and future security agreements should “be structured consistently with defense agreements that exist with our other Western allies and strictly adhere to our human rights laws and values.” He voted against the amendment aimed at cutting off U.S. aid to Israel.

He also recently stepped into the Democratic debate over health care. He told NBC News last month that he doesn’t support “Medicare for All,” the policy preference of many progressives, but later clarified in a radio interview that health care should be “a right available to every single American.” A clip from 2025 recently made the rounds on X with Jeffries saying, “Universal health care is the goal.”

Jeffries’ efforts may already be working. William Lawrence, a progressive House candidate from Michigan who previously said he hoped to be able to vote for a Jeffries alternative for speaker, has since thrown his support behind the New Yorker. Lawrence’s campaign against a Republican incumbent also recently picked up the support of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the official campaign arm of House Democrats.

The left is also getting a glimpse at how Democratic leaders could use their power to constrain dissenters next year. Progressives recoiled from a proposal floated in a caucus meeting earlier this month that could penalize members seeking committee leadership posts for bucking party leadership on procedural votes. Democrats are locked in a debate over what to do after two moderates broke ranks to pass rule votes that helped advance the GOP leadership’s floor agenda. But, as one progressive pointed out, opposing the procedural steps that bring bills up for floor votes are often dissenters’ only point of leverage against leadership.

The tactic only works, however, if a party has a very narrow majority, and both Jeffries and progressives are waiting to see, should Democrats win, what sort of a margin they secure. Ultimately, that’s what progressives believe will decide how much muscle they can flex on the Hill next year.

“If we have a big majority then the voting bloc will have very little power,” one progressive candidate said. “If it’s thin, then [Jeffries] is going to need to negotiate with anyone who has concerns about him having the gavel.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 4
entries.summary: This week’s group features outside hitters from Wootton and Bishop O’Connell and a setter from Flint Hill.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This week’s standouts hail from some of the winningest volleyball teams in the local area. From two outside hitters who have helped their teams to unbeaten starts to a crafty setter quarterbacking one of the most historically dominant programs in the DMV, here’s who earned Player of the Week honors for volleyball in Week 4:

Haile Ma, Senior, Outside Hitter, Wootton

After graduating a bevy of seniors from a Wootton team that advanced to the state quarterfinals last season, the Patriots have leaned on Ma as a steady source of offense at the outside hitter position. Last Friday against Walter Johnson, Ma poured in 19 kills in a four-set victory. Against Bethesda-Chevy Chase days earlier, Ma put down 21 kills in a thrilling five-set win. The senior ended the week averaging nearly 15 kills per match on the season along with 18 total aces and 44 digs.

“I thought the B-CC game was very hard-fought by both teams, and it was a really even match,” Wootton coach Mary Malinauskas said. “I was glad to see my girls hang in there and not panic when it was a five-set match.”

Nadia Wooten, Freshman, Outside Hitter, Bishop O’Connell

O’Connell is the hottest team in the area so far this season. Despite facing a loaded schedule against some of the area’s premier volleyball programs, the Knights have yet to drop a set amid a flawless 21-0 start, including tournament play.

Wooten, a nationally ranked freshman outside hitter, has been a major key to O’Connell’s early success. Against league rival St. John’s last week, she finished with 25 kills to just one error in an impressive victory. Wooten and the Knights will travel to Phoenix for the Nike Tournament of Champions to test their mettle against some of the best programs in the country this week.

“The way [Wooten] plays, you can’t tell she’s a freshman,” Knights coach Mehdi El-Alaoui said. “It’s another level. … She had a phenomenal week.”

Ava Zender, Senior, Setter, Flint Hill

Over the first month of the season, Flint Hill coach Thai Nguyen has watched his team gel into one of the most highly productive offensive teams in the area. Much of the Huskies’ offensive success starts with Zender, whose passing ability sets up the squad’s talented outside hitters to thrive. Last week, Zender helped lead her team to victories over Georgetown Visitation and Collegiate — Zender dished 24 assists in the latter win as Flint Hill picked up its 12th victory.

Zender’s connection with senior Hunter Ross, a UCLA commit, makes the Huskies one of the most feared programs in the area this season.

“We’ll continue leaning towards [Zender] for the rest of the season to make smart decisions,” Nguyen said. “Her mental toughness has really impressed me this year.”

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Oct. 1)
entries.summary: Art on the Avenue in Del Ray, ARTS by George! at George Mason and the March On! Festival.
entries.content:
Thursday 


Story District’s “Top Shelf” at the Lincoln Theatre

1215 U St. NW, 8 p.m., $45

No rail drinks are allowed at “Top Shelf,” a showcase featuring some of the best performances from recent Story District events. In the spirit of The Moth and other like-minded organizations, Story District helps everyday Washingtonians craft first-person narratives eventually performed onstage, from memory. The results are never pure comedy but always cathartic, for performer and audience.

The March On! Festival screens “Declarations”

NCTA, 25 Massachusetts Ave. NW, 6 to 8 p.m., free, donations requested

Day Three of the eight-day film festival focusing on civil rights and the African diaspora includes a screening of the new Virginia Public Media documentary “Declarations: Black Americans and the Revolutionary War,”followed by a discussion with historians, policymakers and director Stacey L. Holman.

More to explore: The Submerge Project digital art exhibition is open at Artechouse.

Friday 


SHAPE in Motion: Art Benefit at the French Embassy  

4101 Reservoir Road NW, 6 to 9 p.m., $18-25

Got a high-brow sk8er boi? Or mademoiselle? Bring them to La Maison Française on Friday, where the embassy grounds will be transformed into an art market and skate park in honor of the upcoming Youth Olympic Games in Senegal. Entertainment includes live DJs, a West African fashion show featuring Howard University students and a demonstration by Zambian pro skater Mukuka Chande.

The National Symphony Orchestra at Strathmore

5301 Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, 8 p.m., $22 to $119

The NSO opens its peripatetic season with concerts at George Mason University (Thursday) and Strathmore’s Music Center (Friday). Music director Gianandrea Noseda will conduct three early 20th century classics: Rimsky-Korsakov’s “Scheherazade,” Mussorgsky’s “Pictures at an Exhibition” and Ravel’s “Boléro.” Pro tip: The NSO set up its own website independent from the Kennedy Center. Use it to keep track of where they are playing and when.

More to explore: “Horkus Forkus” First Friday at Community Forklift in Edmonston

Saturday


Jeff Goldblum and the Mildred Snitzer Orchestra

At George Mason University’s Center for the Arts, 4373 Mason Pond Dr., Fairfax, 8:30 p.m., $75 to $145

The wizard will see you now, if you love jazz and drive to Fairfax. Jeff Goldblum, a star of “Wicked,” “Jurassic Park” and many more, is also a lauded jazz pianist. He brings the swing to the annual ARTS by George! gala concert, which raises scholarship funds for George Mason University students pursuing careers in the performing arts.

Art on the Avenue

Mount Vernon Avenue, Alexandria, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

It’s one of the largest juried art fairs in the region, and definitely the only one with a pie-baking contest in front of the local custard shop. Art on the Avenue brings more than 350 potters, jewelers, fiber artists, candlemakers and more to the Del Ray neighborhood of Alexandria. Music stages and food options also punctuate Mount Vernon Avenue. Free trolley shuttles run from the Potomac Yard and Braddock Road Metro stations.

More to explore: Festival Latinoamericano at Arlington Mill Community Center.

Sunday 


“Counterpoint: Rhapsody in Blue” by Conrad Tao and Caleb Teicher

At the University of Maryland’s Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center,

8270 Alumni Drive, College Park, 3 p.m, $15 to $50

Tap dancer Caleb Teicher and pianist Conrad Tao devise a one-of-a-kind talent show featuring their two-hands/two-feet arrangement of George Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue.” As seen (and heard) on NPR’s Tiny Desk.

“Venus” closes at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company

641 D Street NW, 2 p.m, $20 to $105

The “cosmic dark comedy” stars longtime local favorite actress Kimberly Gilbert as a woman replaying the highlights of her dream relationship, until one night while stargazing, someone ends up in a shallow grave. Steve Yockey (HBO thriller “The Flight Attendant") wrote the play, and new artistic director Reggie D. White directs. 

More to explore: Indigo Girls at The Anthem

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Trayon, Take Two
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 30, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Trayon’s next steps, a reckoning for DCHA and why the Mystics won’t play at Cap One today.

Capital Weather's Daily Digit — 8/10. Not too far off from an ideal fall day. Just a touch too warm and not super dry air. Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

Tuesday may have been the first normal day for Trayon White in weeks, coming off of a hung jury in his federal bribery trial. But the Ward 8 lawmaker’s legal, political and financial woes are far from over, as The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright, Martin Austermuhle and Michael Brice-Saddler report.

D.C.’s top prosecutor has vowed to retry the case against him, while his own council colleagues are quietly at odds over whether to expel him (again) for ethical violations. And White — who represents more than 87,000 people across Southeast D.C. — still has to deal with an array of investigations and lawsuits into his political and personal spending.

The city’s ethics board is still digging into White over the $35,000 in cash he took from D.C. businessman Allieu Kamara. White is also facing questions about $60,000 in public funds he used for his 2022 mayoral campaign that is unaccounted for, and his 2024 reelection campaign is $30,000 in debt.

All those investigations have been on hold pending the outcome of his bribery trial. If prosecutors decide to try him again, those matters will have to wait longer still. That’s frustrating for some of White’s colleagues, who see all of these cases hanging over the city’s legislature.

“The longer this goes on, the longer there is no accountability for what has taken place in a variety of areas,” said At-Large D.C. Council member Christina Henderson. “It does put us in a pattern where nothing is settled. I would like to see resolution.”

As for White, he’s been both cautious and strident. On Monday, he said he was focused on “getting back to the work of being a council member, father, and to my family.” But he also took to social media to jab at U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro, saying: “Trump didn’t fire her yet? Guess she is not tired of losing.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

At-Large council member Robert White called for a targeted forensic audit of the D.C. Housing Authority at an oversight roundtable yesterday to resolve the fraud allegations outlined in a scathing audit this year, when auditors couldn’t verify how much money DCHA had, or where it was, to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. The housing committee roundtable also took up a June cyberattack, when a small subset of data from DCHA’s shared drives was accessed by hackers.

“It is a mess, and it's been a mess for a long time, and the last effort to clean it up made it worse,” Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin said. “We’ve got to be on top of you as much as we can without detracting from your ability to get the work done.”

Crews began moving back the fences surrounding Lafayette Square this week, allowing the public farther into the park in front of the White House than it has been able to get for eight months, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

Dark tint on car windows can get you pulled over in D.C., but a new report from the city’s Office of Police Complaints recommends changes to how and when D.C. police officers stop and cite drivers for it. In short, the report says officers have to have the right equipment to actually measure window tint before deciding to stop someone.

The Kennedy Center has laid off nearly two dozen box office employees as the performing arts institution remains closed and its performance schedule shrinks, City Cast DC reports. It’s the latest staffing cut since President Donald Trump took control of the Kennedy Center. The union says it plans to pursue legal action over the layoffs, which union President Anne Vantine told The Sun “[demonstrate] the organizations' willingness to act in bad faith.”

There’s more: The Nancy Hanks Lecture on Arts and Public Policy is leaving the Kennedy Center — at least for this year. The 36th annual lecture, headlined by Tony Award-winning actress Phylicia Rashad, will take place today at Arena Stage instead.

Come to school, get a free concert ticket? That’s what up to 10,000 D.C. students can earn — as well as merch and e-gift cards — if they track stellar attendance through a new initiative from the Office of the State Superintendent of Education, Monumental Sports and Rang Rewards. While D.C. has reduced its chronic absenteeism rate by 9% since the pandemic, truancy remains a pressing issue. School leaders canapply now for their schools to be part of the pilot cohort, which will launch in January.





FROM VIRGINIA

A Northern Virginia man originally sentenced to death for a 2001 murder was released from prison on Monday as part of a plea deal, InsideNoVa reports.

The Alexandria Police Department will publish a map of all its Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers by Thursday, NBC4 reports.





FROM MARYLAND

More than 1.9 million customers across Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were advised to use water only as absolutely necessary Tuesday.As The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports, an electrical problem at the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission’s Potomac filtration plant stalled its ability to provide its normal water outputs. The plant was able to restore service to normal operating levels Tuesday evening, but it still urged customers to limit their use of non-essential water.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For storytellers: Story District’s “Top Shelf,” Thursday.

For Francophile sk8er bois: SHAPE in Motion, Friday.

For “Wicked” and/or “Independence Day” groupies: Jeff Goldblum and the Mildred Snitzer Orchestra, Saturday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

The Mystics host a do-or-die Game 2 tonight in their playoff series against the Atlanta Dream, and are looking to extend their breakthrough season. But the appropriate location for the game is a matter of fan debate. Washington and Atlanta will face off in CareFirst Arena, the Mystics’ home arena in Southeast. At just 4,200 seats, it’s the smallest venue to host a WNBA game this postseason, which has driven up playoff ticket prices and sparked questions about why the game wasn’t moved to Capital One Arena — home to the Wizards and Capitals. The reason? The Jonas Brothers are booked to play a show there that night.

The Commanders overhauled their roster this offseason, adding starters in free agency and through the draft. Which ones have made the biggest impact through three games? We ranked the top five.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Nikie Johnson, Erik Schutz and Jaden Amos. Yesterday’s trivia answer was A) Bill Clinton, who attended Georgetown University. A special shout-out to Melissa Gray, who answered first. Finally, that three-bedroom townhouse we showed you yesterday is located in D.C., and 11% of you guessed that right. The most common guess was Virginia.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Republicans Make Their AI Move
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Data centers’ day in the Senate. Gun violence and abortion advocates try to get in on the midterm conversation. Inside Jeffries’ effort to turn his Democratic haters. Missouri as a redistricting omen. And: At the MAHA Summit.





THE LATEST

Today is for data center political theater. The Washington Sun’s Elena Schneider and Igor Bobic have all the details on what is sure to be a fun day in the Senate, depending on how you define “fun,” of course.

Republicans are planning to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who has come under withering attacks in his general election fight against former Sen. Sherrod Brown over data center development. The bill, in theory, answers those attacks by directing state public-utility commissions to consider making data centers responsible for their own energy costs. Husted is casting this as an opportunity for data center critics to put their money where their mouth is. “It is the only game in town,” he told reporters yesterday. “It is the only bill that has a chance to get to the president’s desk before we get to the election.”

Democrats’ response is we’ll pass, thanks. “It’s just fakery to try to fool voters into forgetting that Republicans spent the entire term trying to stop states from regulating AI (as requested by the AI companies),” Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) posted on X, reflecting the general take from his caucus. Republicans need seven Democrats to get cloture on this bill, and that does not seem likely.

That’s the theater. As is often the case in the Senate, there will be floor action but probably no surprise outcome. On the one hand, Congress is actually responding to swiftly shifting voter opinion on AI infrastructure. On the other, members know nothing will happen other than rhetoric.

Here’s the politics: Can voting for the bill help Republicans — already on the back foot over AI out on the campaign trail — blunt this potent Democratic political attack? They really need it to, strategists told The Sun. “It’s a tailor-made, perfect shitstorm, combining affordability and corporate corruption and greed,” said one GOP pollster.

More: DOJ Inspector General ‘Declined Further Action’ on Todd Blanche Cryptocurrency Matter • Trump Says the AI Industry Will ‘Self-Police’ Under a New Accord • Hegseth Bars Civilian Faculty Tenure at Military Academies • Karoline Leavitt Discloses Family Investments in Trump Media and Tesla

Open tabs:
  • Americans Want Populist Policies That Defy Traditional Political Labels (WSJ)
  • Officials cast doubt on Trump’s plan for drones, snipers at proposed arch (WaPo)
  • US forces exit Iraq, emboldening Iran’s proxies and Islamic State (Reuters)
  • OpenAI Ignored Employees Who Warned It Wasn’t Doing Enough About Security (NYT)




FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: The down-ballot issue play. Gun violence and abortion access have not rated as central topics this cycle, to say the least — some pollsters have not even listed them among the key questions facing voters. But advocates focused on these issues say they can prove that they matter, flexing their political networks in the final month before the midterms in close races across the country.

Giffords PAC is going live today with three new ads, part of the gun-safety group’s $10 million spend this cycle. Each is designed to move a battleground race: a $1 million effort focused on Republican Mike Bouchard in Michigan’s 10th District; another is part of an $850K spend against Republican Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th; the third is part of a $700K spend against Republican David Valadao in California’s 22nd. All the ads directly mention gun policy, but place it within a context familiar to anyone following ads this cycle — corruption and cost of living.

Reproductive Freedom for All, the abortion-rights group formerly known as NARAL, is out today with endorsements in 21 races, including six where Democrats are trying to flip Republican-held seats. The group says it’s mobilizing Americans who support abortion rights and want to vote on the issue.

New polling gives that idea some merit. Fresh polling from abortion-rights group Abortion Access Now found 59% of voters disagree with the Supreme Court’s ruling overturning Roe v. Wade, including big majorities across key groups like independents, swing voters and suburban women. The poll was conducted to mark the 50th anniversary of the Hyde Amendment, and found 67% of registered voters support Medicaid coverage of reproductive care including abortion — that’s a five-point bump from a similar poll taken in 2019.

More: ‘Love Me’ Artist Threatens Legal Action Over Taxpayer-Funded Trump Ad  



FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Hakeem Jeffries’ bridge-building: If Democrats win the House, their majority will include a decent number of progressives who have publicly promised never to vote for a Speaker Jeffries. There is already an effort underway to change their minds, The Sun’s Stephen Neukam reports. Jeffries has now spoken with all the progressives who won their primaries, and has met with or plans to meet with them all in person, Stephen writes. Reps. Joe Neguse of Colorado and Lauren Underwood of Illinois, two members of Jeffries’ leadership team, have also been reaching out.

Is this effort working? Progressive upset primary winner William Lawrence, now the Democratic nominee in a swing Michigan district, recently backed off his public skepticism toward Jeffries and said he would support him for speaker.





THE BIG ONE

No lessons from Missouri’s misery: “If Republicans do it, the Democrats are going to respond, and if the Democrats respond, then the Republicans respond again,” Rep. Emanuel Cleaver — the Democrat whipsawed by the back-and-forth-and-back-again redistricting fight in the state — told The Sun’s Manuela Silva of what he learned from the experience. “Everybody then begins to fight fire with fire, but in the end, nothing is left but silt and ash and burnt cinders.”

Cleaver is not a fan of this, and does not recommend others try it. Manuela has covered the legal fight over Missouri’s congressional lines extensively, and has a big story up today about what it means for the next month in the state: Cleaver and other lawmakers saw their lines get changed multiple times, and voters who cast ballots in one district in the August primary will cast them in different districts in November. It’s pretty messy.

It’s also what the rest of the country can look forward to. No one on either side sees a quiet end to the mid-cycle redistricting the Trump team kicked off. “I think people will continue to do it,” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida) told Manuela yesterday. Democrats said the same thing.





THE WASHINGTON SUN CAST

From your favorite podcast app: “It might be that people are just so fed up that they want to toss their incumbent out,” congressional reporter Paul Kane says about the state of this year’s midterms and candidates who could be in trouble.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

What the MAHA Summit was like: Senior Trump administration officials mingled for hours with health and wellness industry officials and MAHA activists who are concerned over vaccines, processed food and chronic illness, The Sun’s Paige Winfield Cunningham reports from her day at the D.C. event celebrating the movement Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. brought to Washington.

There were some signs MAHA still doesn’t feel entirely comfortable in the mainstream GOP. Corporate partners were everywhere. Leaders of UnitedHealth and AHIP, the insurer association, participated in a panel about affordability. Standard politics stuff — that did not sit well with some.

“I think it’s a little bit of a challenge that the presentations on the stage seemed to be about bureaucracy being big business,” Florida nurse Kate Johnson, who attended the White House event last year announcing its MAHA report, told Paige yesterday. “That’s not the core of what the MAHA movement is.”



More: Appeals Court Rejects Trump Effort to Stay Sanctions in IRS Lawsuit • Lithuania ‘Ready’ to Foot the Bill to Permanently Host U.S. Troops, Prime Minister Says • Some Judges Sound Open to Restarting Contempt Probe in El Salvador Deportation Case





NOT US

  • “A Massive Power Grab”: White House Proposal Threatens Funding That Helps Disabled Americans Vote, by Lisa Song for ProPublica
  • Democrats are running pastors for office. Republicans are attacking their religious comments. By Samuel Benson for Politico
  • How the Pentagon Is Escalating Trump’s Drug War in Latin America, by Shelby Holliday, Vera Bergengruen and Lara Seligman for The Wall Street Journal

entries.title: Missouri Is a Nightmare Come True for Redistricting Opponents
entries.summary: Because of legal battles over district lines, some of the state’s voters will cast a ballot in a different district in November than they did in the primary.
entries.content:
Rep. Emanuel Cleaver has had the most convoluted reelection campaign imaginable.

In early September, he was campaigning in a newly redrawn district meant to heavily tilt the seat to Republicans. Then, a state Supreme Court ruling reverted his seat to its previous boundaries, which overwhelmingly favored his campaign. Another court reversed that call.

And on Friday, following weeks of back-and-forth, the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in for a third time to reverse that ruling, putting Cleaver back in a strong position to keep his seat, which encompasses nearly all of Kansas City.

He heard the news from Rep. Wesley Bell, the one other Democrat in the Missouri congressional delegation, and immediately pulled over on the side of the road. “Rev, we won!” Cleaver recalled Bell telling him on the phone.

Thanks to that order, Cleaver is likely to win in November. But he considers what happened in his state more of a cautionary tale than a victory in the broader redistricting fight.

“I think everybody should agree with no mid-decade redistricting, because if we do [it], we're just going to continue to tear this nation apart,” Cleaver told The Washington Sun on Monday. “If Republicans do it, the Democrats are going to respond, and if the Democrats respond, then the Republicans respond again. Everybody then begins to fight fire with fire, but in the end, nothing is left but silt and ash and burnt cinders.”

“The rest of the nation needs to look at what happened in Missouri, and say, ‘That’s what we don’t want in our state,’” Cleaver said.

The legal battle over Missouri’s map was a nightmare come true for many of the people who warned that redistricting would set off an expensive and chaotic battle between the two parties for years to come.

The congressional map that Missouri Republicans drew up last fall would have split a compact, city-centered district into three. It would have made driving across the 5th Congressional District a multihour trek instead of a 45-minute one. And it would have turned Cleaver’s race, which he’s won with more than 51% of the vote each cycle since 2012, into one that he would have likely lost to state Sen. Rick Brattin, who is backed by President Donald Trump.

It was according to those redrawn lines that voters cast their primary ballots. Now, some voters will ctast their ballots in a different district in November than the one they did in August.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state that took action to redraw its congressional maps after Trump called on state lawmakers to make their districts more GOP-friendly last year. Republicans targeted Cleaver’s district, moving to make Troost Avenue — a street with a history of being a racial dividing line — into a district boundary.

After Gov. Mike Kehoe signed the new maps, the advocacy group People Not Politicians Missouri submitted a petition to Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in December challenging the changes. Unlike many other states, Missouri allows voters to dispute laws by collecting enough signatures to force a statewide vote on a bill.

Hoskins, a Republican, waited until the last possible day to announce his decision not to certify the signatures challenging the maps. That coincided with the state’s primary elections on Aug. 4, which were set up according to the redrawn lines.

A flurry of state and federal lawsuits have been filed in the back-and-forth over the Republican-friendly maps — including two filed against Hoskins in recent weeks by voters seeking damages. People Not Politicians filed a lawsuit that would give voters a chance to approve the new maps this November while keeping the old maps in place in the meantime.

Two of the lawsuits escalated to the U.S Supreme Court, which three times set back the Republican efforts to implement their new map in the fall.

“The big picture from Missouri is that people are going to resist power grabs,” said Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians. “People understand what a power grab is, particularly one that is emanating from Washington, D.C.”

Hoskins, who at one point was found in contempt of court for proceeding under the redrawn maps, did not respond to a request for comment. Brattin, Cleaver’s Republican challenger, also did not respond to a request for comment.

As the court challenges played out, Missouri became the center of the broader conversation about the politics of redistricting clashing with the need for voters to know where they would cast their ballots, days into absentee voting. In early September, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) told The Sun that the state needed “clarity as soon as possible.”

When the ruling came, however, Hawley said he wasn’t surprised.

“Look, I was in favor of the 7-1 map,” Hawley said on Tuesday. “I’d love to have more Republicans.”

Asked if Republicans should continue to redistrict for 2028, Hawley said that “it’s totally up to the states.” “They can do it how they want to do it. I supported Missouri's effort, and you know I'm sure blue states will keep trying to add blue seats, and red states will try to add red seats, and we'll see. I mean, we'll see this November, I mean, voters either way are going to have the say in the end,” he said, pointing to the measure now on the ballot in Missouri.

Meanwhile, Democrats have responded with their own map redrawing efforts elsewhere.

“We’re not going to unilaterally disarm,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told The Sun in early September. “This is not over. We’re just getting started until there is a national law that prohibits mid-decade redistricting.”

Many other states are already setting themselves up to redraw their lines ahead of 2028.

In Maryland and New York, Democrats were able to include ballot measures this year that would make it easier to redraw their state’s congressional lines ahead of the next election cycle. And a slew of Republican-led legislatures — including in Missouri and a handful of Southern states with majority-minority districts that were weakened by the Supreme Court’s gutting of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act earlier this year — have made clear they’re looking into where they can keep redrawing maps to their advantage, too.

“We're living in an era of perpetual redistricting,” John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, told The Sun. “Republicans have shown no willingness to slow down, especially if Democrats do perform well in this midterm. Republicans are going to try and go back to the well and find everything they can. We're preparing for that, and we'll be willing and ready to engage and fight back against everything that they're going to try and throw at us.”

There’s been talk of Congress taking steps to ban mid-decade redistricting, but they’ve gotten little traction. California Rep. Kevin Kiley, who announced in March that he was dropping his affiliation to the Republican Party and becoming an independent after Democratic redistricting in his state made his race more competitive, said redistricting is “mutually assured destruction” where “everyone loses.”

“It’s not benefiting anyone and most people agree with me on that,” Kiley told The Sun. “It’s just the leadership on both sides has been unwilling to do anything about it.”

After having such a close brush with getting drawn out of Congress, Cleaver told The Sun that he plans to introduce a ban on mid-decade redistricting — something that Kiley did last year after Democrats targeted his seat.

In Missouri, Republicans pushed until the last minute to be able to use their redrawn lines. Election officials began mailing absentee ballots to voters even as a court decision was pending, and the litigation continued as workers warned that further changes could cause irreversible chaos.

“Any further change inflicts additional vertigo on local election authorities—and the millions of Missourians who rely on them—after ostensibly-final resolution consistent with Missouri law," a group of county clerks and election authorities wrote in a brief filed on Sept. 15.

Following Friday’s high court decision, Missouri voters will cast ballots based on the 2022 map and decide on whether they want to use the Republican redrawn map — the one that draws out Cleaver’s seat — in future elections, under a ballot measure known as Proposition A.

Cleaver thinks the ongoing redistricting efforts will continue to cause problems, even though he knows it's unlikely to stop.

“I haven't gone anywhere with Republicans or Democrats where I have heard people say, ‘Boy, this is really nice. This is really, really a good thing,’” he said. “Nobody likes this, and so why would we continue to do something that we know the American public finds distasteful, and it damages our ability to govern?”

entries.title: Trayon White’s First Trial Is Over. The Political Saga Is Not.
entries.summary: It remains unclear whether White will be retried, whether his fellow council members will vote to expel him and how he’ll contend with an array of investigations, lawsuits and personal debts.
entries.content:
On Tuesday, for the first business day in more than two weeks, D.C. Council member Trayon White was free to go about his work and life without stepping foot in the city’s federal courthouse.

But the Ward 8 lawmaker’s legal, political and financial woes are far from over, even though his first bribery trial ended Monday in a hung jury. D.C.’s top prosecutor has vowed to retry the case against him. His colleagues on the council are quietly at odds over whether to expel him again for ethical violations. And the lawmaker, who represents 87,000 residents across Southeast D.C., must still contend with an array of investigations and lawsuits involving his political spending and personal debts.

What’s more: Many of these matters won’t be resolved until White’s criminal proceedings conclude — meaning White, the rest of the council and the various government bodies investigating him are all stuck in an uncomfortable limbo with no clear end in sight.

“The longer this goes on, the longer there is no accountability for what has taken place in a variety of areas,” said D.C. Council member Christina Henderson (I-At Large). “It does put us in a pattern where nothing is settled. I would like to see resolution.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

White, who claims former D.C. “mayor for life” Marion Barry as a political mentor, has grown a loyal following in his home ward by being highly visible and responsive to the concerns of ordinary people. But his legal troubles exploded into public view two years ago, in August 2024, when he was arrested outside his Navy Yard apartment complex and charged with bribery. Authorities allege that White accepted $35,000 in cash bribes and agreed to accept more than $150,000 in exchange for agreeing to help a local businessman secure D.C. government grants.

White’s defense attorneys did not dispute that he took the money.

But the issue for prosecutors is that while D.C. government officials did testify that White had approached them about his associate’s work with the city, no one testified that White had actually pressured them to extend his contracts. And, as appeals courts have upheld over the years, a bribery conviction requires the government to prove that, in addition to taking the money, White actually intended to exert his influence to get those contracts extended.

“That’s a hard thing to prove without him having gone out there and having done it,” said Georgetown University Law Center professor Erica Hashimoto. “The government has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt what was in his head.”

White claimed in an Instagram post Tuesday that the jury had voted 9-3 in favor of acquittal; his attorney Gary Kohlman confirmed the same count to The Washington Sun. A spokesperson for the U.S. attorney for D.C. did not respond to a request for comment.

Shortly after U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras declared a mistrial, U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro said her office would seek to retry the case. White’s defense attorneys have also filed a motion for summary judgment of acquittal, arguing that prosecutors did not bring enough evidence for a reasonable jury to convict White and asking Contreras to acquit their client from the bench.

If Contreras does not acquit White, the government can try again with a new jury — likely with the same evidence, unless a helpful new witness happens to emerge, Hashimoto said.

***

In the meantime, questions are swirling about White’s future on the council, which could still expel him over ethical violations — and White’s colleagues are offering little clarity in response.

The D.C. Council’s chair, Phil Mendelson, said lawmakers would wait for the outcome of the legal process before deciding whether to proceed with an expulsion of White. “We need finality here,” he said, adding that lawmakers were divided on whether ejecting White was even the right decision. The council unanimously voted to expel White after he was indicted. He was subsequently reelected in the special election to fill the seat he vacated, though he earned less than a third of the vote in a crowded, low-turnout race.

Most Council members declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Others did comment. Charles Allen (D-Ward 6) said in a statement that White’s disregard of ethics continues to “embarrass the institution of the Council” but declined to say directly whether he supports another expulsion vote. Elissa Silverman (I-At Large) said in a diplomatic statement that the council should both respect the legal process and redouble efforts to bolster trust in city government. Robert White Jr. (D-At Large) said in a statement that the council should allow White’s legal process to continue “without prejudging the outcome.”

Henderson, in an interview Tuesday, said she wants the council to act on a bill she introduced in June 2025 that would prohibit any council member who is expelled by their colleagues from serving for five years. Currently there is no such prohibition, which White benefited from when he was reelected to his Ward 8 seat in July 2025 — some seven months after he was expelled by his colleagues.

“We do still have a gaping loophole that this situation has pointed to, and instead of acting on it we are doing what Congress does: We notice a problem and we still don’t do anything about it,” she said.

Patrick Mara, the chair of the District of Columbia Republican Party, said he wants the council to act immediately to boot White from office.

“It shouldn’t matter your party, it shouldn’t matter your ideology within that party … this is wrong and the council really needs to move on this, because until it does there really will be a dark cloud over the D.C. Council,” he said.

While White remains on the council, there is also a question of how much influence he can have on legislation and government oversight. While he previously chaired the council’s committee on youth affairs, which oversees several offices including the city’s juvenile justice agency, Mendelson stripped him of that leadership role after his indictment. In an interview Monday, Mendelson stood by the decision: “My own view is that somebody with ethical issues should not be rewarded with a committee chairmanship,” he said.

Among White’s supporters, there’s a strong desire to move on.

“Hopefully this is a reset … for him, for all of us,” said Derek Floyd, who founded the youth-focused nonprofit Crowns Incorporated and attended the trial proceedings in solidarity with White.

***

Even if he gets out from under the criminal case, and even if the council does not expel him, White faces other potential trouble.

First, there’s a pending investigation by the D.C. Board of Ethics and Government Accountability over White’s likely violation of the council ethics rules that prohibit elected officials from accepting gifts from contractors who do business with the city, along with a separate city ethics law that requires disclosure of any such gifts and recusal from any related votes or actions thereafter. The government body could levy fines on White if it finds he violated the rules.

White is also facing outstanding fines from his unsuccessful run for D.C. mayor in 2022 — and questions about public campaign funds that remain unaccounted for.

During that campaign, White participated in the city’s Fair Elections Program, which offers matching public funds for contributions that D.C. residents make to a candidate. White received more than $435,000 in public funds for his campaign, but in March 2024 the D.C. Office of Campaign Finance determined that $59,000 remained unaccounted for. Under D.C. law, any funds that remain after a race ends have to be returned to the city. White was fined $18,100 for failing to return the money and other campaign finance violations.

The investigation — which was put on hold after White was indicted in August 2024 — could eventually resume, requiring White to fully account for the public funds he never returned and the fine he hasn’t yet paid.

“When a criminal matter is pending against a respondent before our office, it is our standard practice to grant a continuance until the criminal matter has been fully resolved,” wrote spokesperson Wesley Williams in an email to The Sun.

White also has outstanding debt from his 2024 reelection campaign, which he had to run without the benefit of public funding because of the ongoing questions around his 2022 mayoral bid. He owes more than $30,000 to a number of vendors. Under D.C. law, that debt — which is now owed by his campaign committee — could transfer to him personally.

Those financial penalties and debts could add to an already difficult financial situation for White, who said in one of the FBI recordings played at trial that he was “bankrupt.” An IRS agent testified at trial that prior to his arrest, one of White’s checking accounts was overdrawn by $1,000.

In the midst of the legal and political morass, White’s public demeanor has alternated between cautious and strident. He said at a news conference Monday that he was not gloating after the mistrial. Approached by a reporter Monday night, White responded to Pirro’s pledge to retry him by saying he was focused on returning to his life.

“At this time, I am focusing on my innocence and getting back to the work of being a council member, father and to my family,” he said, sitting quietly with a group of people at Sycamore and Oak in Southeast D.C.

The next day, however, he took a different approach — including a direct response to Pirro.

“Trump didn’t fire her yet? Guess she is not tired of losing,” White wrote on social media. “No quid pro quo. Never was and never will be. My God is bigger than the United States Government.”
entries.author: Jenny Gathright, Martin Austermuhle, Michael Brice-Saddler

entries.title: Why Didn’t the Mystics Playoff Game Get Moved to Capital One?
entries.summary: The answer is more than just “The Jonas Brothers.”
entries.content:
The most elusive WNBA playoff ticket is not found in Indianapolis or New York or Dallas. Instead? Nowhere is harder (or more expensive) to get in than D.C.

When the Mystics host Game 2 of the first round on Wednesday, they will do so at their usual home of CareFirst Arena in Southeast D.C., which is among the smallest in the WNBA with a capacity of just 4,200. It will be the smallest arena hosting a playoff game in the league this year.

The only team with a smaller home than the Mystics is their current playoff opponent, the Atlanta Dream, but they have moved their postseason games so far to a much larger facility in State Farm Arena, ordinarily the home of the NBA’s Hawks. But a similar move will not be made this round for the Mystics to play at Capital One Arena, the home of the Wizards and Capitals.

The low capacity for a big game has contributed to high prices for the Mystics’ first playoff home game since 2019. As of Tuesday morning, fans could get in the door of every other upcoming WNBA playoff game for no more than $65, according to Ticketmaster. Meanwhile, the cheapest Mystics ticket available was $192.88. (That number was even higher before the Mystics’ loss in Game 1 on Sunday.)

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Fans were quick to react to the prices — and the fact that Capitol One is hosting a Jonas Brothers concert the night of the game.

“I mean, good for [the Mystics],” one user wrote, “but … can the Jonas brothers cancel their concert?”

There are larger facilities in the region that have previously hosted the Mystics, including Capital One. (The Mystics, Capitals and Wizards are all owned by Monumental Sports and Entertainment.) While the arena was closed for renovations this summer, it reopened in late September, and the Mystics played their last game of the regular season there.

In response to questions from The Washington Sun about whether management considered blocking off Capital One for potential WNBA playoff dates or whether there had been any discussion of moving the concert, Monumental Sports and Entertainment replied with a statement:

“Capital One Arena hosts more than 200 events on average each year, including full home schedules for three team tenants, world-class concerts and a wide range of special events — all while continuing the transformation of the arena. Dates and venue needs must be coordinated across several teams, leagues, promoters and other partners, often months or years in advance. We will continue working closely with the Mystics and the league to identify opportunities to host Mystics games at Capital One Arena in future seasons.”

The Mystics have played most of their home games at CareFirst since 2019. (Previously, they played at Capital One, where strong attendance in their early years dipped as the league struggled in the late 2000s and early 2010s.) The building is owned and operated by the city government through Events DC. It also serves as the Wizards’ practice facility and as the home of the G League Capital City Go-Go.

As the WNBA has grown over the last few years, Washington’s arena has become the subject of increased discussion. By next year, 10 of the 15 WNBA teams will be playing in NBA or NHL arenas that seat at least 15,000. (Another three are in arenas with a capacity of more than 10,000.) CareFirst Arena’s size made it something of an outlier in the WNBA even when it was brand new. It has only become more so in the years since. Every home game for the Mystics at CareFirst has been sold out since 2024.

Their lease to play in the building runs through 2037.

But that has previously come up for debate. Monumental proposed moving the team into a bigger arena just a few years ago. In 2023, when the organization tried moving the Wizards and Capitals to a new facility in Virginia, part of the plan involved moving the Mystics to Capital One. Ownership described the franchise as growing too fast to stay in place for long.

“Fortunately, women’s sports are ascendent, experiencing significant growth. The Mystics regularly sell out their home games,” Monumental CEO Ted Leonsis wrote in a January 2024 letter about the proposal. “Unfortunately, the Mystics and its dedicated fan base are outgrowing the Entertainment and Sports Arena,” the old name of CareFirst.

The D.C. government pushed back on the team leaving the arena before the expiration of the lease. Ultimately, the plan was scuttled in March 2024, and Monumental instead reached a deal with D.C. to keep the Capitals and Wizards at Capital One Arena until 2050. That has left the Mystics in place at CareFirst.

Wednesday night will mark the first home playoff game for the franchise since the 2019 WNBA Finals. (The Mystics qualified for the playoffs in 2022 and ’23 but were swept out of the first round both times before having the chance to host a game.) In a best-of-three series, Wednesday’s Game 2 is do-or-die for Washington, who pulled off a remarkable turnaround this year. The Mystics say they expect their small house to be very full and very, very loud.

“You feed off that energy and that enthusiasm,” head coach Sydney Johnson said at practice on Tuesday. “D.C. loves this team.”
entries.author: Emma Baccellieri

entries.title: Ranking the Commanders’ Five Most Impactful Newcomers
entries.summary: After three games, which offseason arrivals have fared best for Washington?
entries.content:
The Commanders were plenty active this offseason, making a number of free agent signings — particularly on defense — and upgrading through the draft, including with the No. 7 overall pick.

Which newcomers have made the biggest impact through three weeks? Here’s our ranking:

1. Amik Robertson, Defensive Back

The Commanders added so many new faces to their defense that Robertson’s arrival may have been overlooked. But he has brought stability to the Commanders’ secondary, especially in light of fellow cornerback Mike Sainristil’s recent struggles.

Tasked with covering Seahawks star wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba in Sunday’s upset win, Robertson had four pass deflections and a forced fumble. His six deflections for the season put him among the league’s leaders. In addition to thriving in pass coverage, Robertson has also shown an ability to contribute against the run.

“He’s been an excellent addition to our group,” Commanders coach Dan Quinn said on Sunday of Robertson. “For him, coming up like he did, there was a giant chip on his shoulder. And what’s cool about it, it ain’t never left. He is one of those guys that is down for the fight.”

2. Sonny Styles, Linebacker

The rookie out of Ohio State has been as good as advertised, making himself an early candidate for Defensive Rookie of the Year. On Sunday he recorded an interception and a forced fumble, and he previously had a sack in the season opener against the Eagles (trucking Philadelphia star running back Saquon Barkley in the process). The former All-American is already a versatile part of Quinn’s defense, proving he can contribute to the pass rush, drop back in coverage and tackle.

“He’s capable of producing the ball based on the speed and length,” Quinn said of Styles. “For that to come to fruition, that was a big deal.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

3. Stefon Diggs, Wide Receiver

Diggs has brought experience to a receiver room that doesn’t have much outside of Terry McLaurin, and has provided an early boost to the offense (despite his costly unsportsmanlike conduct penalty in the season opener). He is second on the team in receiving yards with 135, and has three touchdowns in as many games.

“I liked the fire that he has in him,” Quinn said in August. “I knew he was good [in] zones. He's probably better in beating the man-to-man than I thought just from the good route running. But I do like the competitor a lot. I really do.”

4. K'Lavon Chaisson, Edge Rusher

General manager Adam Peters looked to address the team’s pass rush, or lack thereof, after last season, and Chaisson has been a strong and consistent threat. In free agency, Chaisson turned down a three-year contract with the Saints to sign a one-year, $11 million deal with Washington in an attempt to get a bigger contract next year. So far the bet he made on himself is paying off.

He entered Sunday’s game with an 18.6% pressure rate, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, which is the best among the Commanders’ primary pass rushers. While Chaisson only has one sack on the season, he had a tackle-for-loss and quarterback hit against the Seahawks.

5. Rachaad White, Running Back

White returned on Sunday after suffering a shoulder injury in the middle of the game and had a 19-yard run with less than two minutes left to help seal the win. He also scored a six-yard receiving touchdown in the first half.

While White is better known for his work on passing downs, he had an efficient Week 2 against the Cowboys, rushing for 43 yards on seven carries.

entries.title: Republicans Confront a Data Center ‘Shitstorm’ in the Midterms
entries.summary: They hope a vote in the Senate Wednesday on a Jon Husted bill will provide an umbrella.
entries.content:
No one wants to be a poster child for data centers anymore, least of all Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

He will get a chance to avert that fate Wednesday with a vote in the Senate to pass a largely symbolic bill aimed at protecting consumers from the power-hungry facilities and, Republicans hope, neutralizing what’s lately become a worrying political anchor.

The giant energy-intensive installations had been hailed as economic boons by many local leaders, but vast swaths of the public now blame them for driving up electricity bills and harming people’s quality of life, all for the benefit of faraway billionaires seen as pushing dangerous artificial intelligence. They are primed to be one of the defining issues of the election.

Husted has faced withering attacks from Democrats over his support for investments and tax incentives for data centers during his tenure as the state’s lieutenant governor. Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, Husted’s Democratic opponent who’s seeking a return to the Senate next year, has dubbed the senator “the face of data centers” in Ohio, and has spent millions of dollars on ads to make the charge stick.

And later this month, LCV Victory Fund, the political action committee of the League of Conservation Voters, will spend another $2 million, hammering Husted on data centers in campaign ads, the group confirmed Tuesday.

Republican leadership, eyeing the close race in ruby-red Ohio, felt concerned enough to keep the Senate in session this week to vote on Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act. The legislation, which sailed through the House in a huge 417-3 vote, would direct state public utility commissions to consider making data centers responsible for their own energy costs, and give lawmakers a way to answer the pressing concern for voters.

“This is our only opportunity, literally, to have something on the president's desk that's a bipartisan vote that will require data centers to build their own infrastructure and give ratepayers relief,” Husted told reporters Tuesday. “It is the only game in town. It is the only bill that has a chance to get to the president's desk before we get to the election.”

But Senate Democrats view Husted’s proposal as little more than an empty promise since it’s states that set electricity rates and the legislation wouldn’t actually require them to do anything. They blocked Husted’s attempt to pass it quickly on the Senate floor last week, and are expected to unite against it again before lawmakers leave town.

“The bill is a fraud,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Tuesday. “The bill is optional. Here we need some real actions on data centers, and what does the Republican senator from Ohio come up with: something that is optional.”

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) said in a post on X: “It's just fakery to try to fool voters into forgetting that Republicans spent the entire term trying to stop states from regulating AI (as requested by the AI companies).”

Republicans believe Wednesday’s procedural vote, which will require 60 senators to advance, including at least seven Democrats, will help Husted and other vulnerable Republican senators up for reelection this year — even if it fails.

“It’s an important message to send to voters that we’re listening to their concerns,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said in an interview. “It’s not too late to be able to spread that message. It’ll be interesting to see what the Democrats choose to do. If they vote against it, then I think that’s a clear contrast for the election.”

Whether a failed vote will make for a meaningful contrast is debatable. But public sentiment against the rapid surge in data infrastructure is not.

Voters’ disapproval for data centers skyrocketed over the last year, shifting from what was initially a locally focused issue to a national debate roiling state and congressional races across the country. The about-face in public opinion prompted candidates in both parties to redefine their positions, including potential 2028 presidential candidates, and across the country it has spurred a flood of campaign ads particularly harmful to Republicans

“It’s a tailor-made, perfect shitstorm, combining affordability and corporate corruption and greed,” said one GOP pollster, granted anonymity to speak candidly and citing both data centers and AI as among the biggest concerns for voters this fall. “Every ad says, ‘Our energy bills are high because this candidate gave data centers a sweetheart deal,’ and it's a very, very powerful message.”

And for Republicans, this pollster said, it’s a “net negative” compared with Democrats because “Republicans are in charge right now.”

The reversal among voters happened quickly. Last year, polling from HeatMap found Americans evenly split over whether they’d back a data center being built nearby. Now, 75% said they’d oppose one. That’s echoed in findings from Gallup and the Pew Research Center, which also found data centers hemorrhaging support.

Private polling, conducted by another Democratic super PAC and obtained by The Washington Sun, drew similar responses. In Ohio’s 15th Congressional District, 75% of voters disapprove of data center development and 23% favor it.

LCV Victory Fund also conducted private polling on data centers — shared with The Sun — and found in January that 44% of voters blamed data centers and artificial intelligence for rising energy costs. By July, 75% said data centers were driving up their energy bills. Sara Schreiber, LCV Victory Fund’s director, said the swing in public opinion has been “extremely dramatic” and that “voters of pretty much every background are extremely fed up with Big Tech.”

Husted is hardly the only Republican lawmaker looking to diffuse that bipartisan frustration — even as the party’s most visible figure, President Donald Trump, vocally supports the projects needed to support AI.

Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Michigan), who’s running in a hotly contested race, flagged in an interview this weekend that he has “disagreed with the president around data centers,” airing TV ads highlighting his assertions that he “stood up to my own party” and “voted against giving your tax dollars to data centers.” He’s one of several Republicans who have called for local control over the facilities.

But Democrats are looking to tie Republicans like Barrett back to their votes on Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which included tax breaks for tech companies.

Schrieber’s group is running ads in six House districts, including in Michigan’s 7th, blaming the officeholders for taking “data center money” and giving data centers “a tax break.”

“Voters are looking for who they can trust on this, and I don’t think they’ve made up their mind on it yet,” Schrieber said. “What is true is that the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress had a lot of chances to do something on this, set a different tone, hold these companies accountable, and they not only passed on that, but they also decided to give massive tax breaks to the companies.”

In Arizona, Jonathan Nez, a Democrat running for a GOP-leaning Arizona seat, is pledging to claw back “the billions in tax breaks” that Republican Rep. Eli Crane “gave the data centers.” In an interview, the former Navajo president said the issue has touched a nerve with voters because “the folks that are pushing data centers are large corporations” and “there's a negative perspective on the billionaires and the wealthy, the elite in this country.”

“Some of these data centers that are being built right now, folks didn't know about it, and now once they find out what's happening, they feel like they've been lied to,” he said.

A spokesman for Crane, in an emailed statement, called Nez “a political insider who’s cozied up to big wind and solar corporations threatening Rural Arizona’s land” and “now he’s attacking me to cover his own tracks.”

Not every Republican candidate is running away from the massive technological build-outs. In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton, who has struggled in his race for Senate, suggested building data centers in rural parts of the country.

“There’s plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centers,” Paxton said at an event this week.

Still, most Republicans believe their party needs to be more sensitive to voter concerns about data centers, even if Husted’s bill won’t necessarily result in lower electricity costs before the November elections.

“I think it's more of a confidence builder,” Cornyn said. “You know, people worry about things that may not come true, but I think everybody's sort of on the same page from the president on down that these power, these data centers, shouldn't raise electricity rates. They don't have independent power. So I think trying to reinforce that message is a good one.”
entries.author: Igor Bobic, Elena Schneider

entries.title: DOJ Inspector General ‘Declined Further Action’ on Todd Blanche Cryptocurrency Matter
entries.summary: The attorney general has faced questions over scuttling crypto investigations while invested in Bitcoin and Ethereum.
entries.content:
The Department of Justice’s Office of the Inspector General “declined further action” on an undisclosed matter involving Attorney General Todd Blanche’s cryptocurrency trades, according to a new federal financial disclosure document reviewed by The Washington Sun.

The revelation of the inspector general’s involvement comes months after ProPublica reported that Blanche — President Donald Trump’s one-time personal lawyer and previous deputy attorney general — torpedoed Biden-era federal investigations into cryptocurrency companies while himself owning six-figures worth of Bitcoin, Ethereum and other digital tokens.

Blanche’s actions prompted a complaint from the watchdog group Campaign Legal Center, which suggested Blanche “blatantly” stood to profit from ending the investigations and called for an inspector general inquiry.

“If Blanche participated in a particular matter affecting the digital asset industry while owning digital assets, he may have violated his ethics agreement and the criminal conflict of interest law,” the complaint read.

A DOJ spokesperson cast the complaint as “baseless character assassination” in a January statement to ProPublica.

It’s unclear the extent to which the DOJ’s inspector general investigated Blanche or otherwise reviewed the matter this year.

The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment for this story. Patrick Shepherd, spokesperson for the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, which published Blanche’s financial disclosure, declined to comment on the matter, saying that the office “does not respond to questions about specific individuals.”

Office of Government Ethics official Scott de la Vega, who signed off on Blanche’s public financial disclosure report, noted on Sept. 2 that the DOJ inspector general’s involvement pertained to seven of Blanche’s cryptocurrency holdings.

In an earlier ethics filing, DOJ Ethics Program Specialist Monica Felter wrote that four of Blanche’s crypto assets — Bitcoin, Solana, Cardano and Ethereum — were “gifted in their entirety” to his grandchildren and adult children in late May 2025 and early June 2025.

Blanche held between $158,010 and $470,000 in various cryptocurrencies before the divestment, largely in Bitcoin and Ethereum.

Federal law only requires government officials to disclose the value of stock, bond and cryptocurrency assets in broad ranges.
